title: Amos
subtitle: Amos, “Burden-bearer”
description: The words of a herdsman from Tekoa whom the LORD sent north to the royal sanctuary at Bethel, in the prosperous reign of Jeroboam II, to tell a wealthy and very religious people that God had seen what their comfort cost the poor. Crime upon crime of the nations, and then Israel’s own; “You alone have I known”; the cows of Bashan; “Prepare to meet your God”; “Seek me and live!”; the festivals God hates, and the cry “let justice roll on like water”; visions of locusts, fire, a plumb line and a basket of summer fruit; a famine of hearing the word of the LORD; and, at the end, the fallen booth of David raised up again. Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Amos?
qa.answer: The third of the twelve shorter prophetic books of the Old Testament, and one of the earliest prophetic books to be written down. In nine chapters it pronounces judgment on Israel’s neighbours and then on Israel itself (chapters 1–2), gathers Amos’s sermons against injustice, empty worship and complacency (3–6), and records five visions, with the story of Amos’s clash with the priest of Bethel (7–9). It ends with a promise that God will raise up “the fallen booth of David” and plant his people in their land for good.

qa.question: Who was Amos, and when did he prophesy?
qa.answer: A herdsman and sheep breeder from Tekoa, a village in Judah south of Bethlehem, who also took care of sycamore-fig trees. He insisted, “I am not a prophet, nor a member of a company of prophets” (7:14): the LORD took him from the flock and sent him to the northern kingdom of Israel. The book dates his words to the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, “two years before the earthquake” (1:1), which most scholars place around 760 BC. His name probably comes from a Hebrew word for carrying a load, which is why it is often explained as “burden-bearer”.

qa.question: What does “let justice roll on like water” mean?
qa.answer: In Amos 5:24 God answers Israel’s crowded festivals and loud songs by saying that he wants something else: “let justice roll on like water, and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry.” In a land where most streambeds dry up in summer, it is a call for justice that never fails, for the poor and for everyone, in the courts and the markets. Martin Luther King Jr. took up the verse in his 1963 speech in Washington, and it has been quoted in the cause of justice ever since.

qa.question: Why does God reject Israel’s worship in Amos?
qa.answer: Not because worship is wrong, but because the worshippers were oppressing the poor. Amos’s hearers brought sacrifices and tithes and sang to the harp, while they sold “the needy for a pair of sandals” (2:6), took bribes in court and cheated with dishonest scales. So God says, “I hate, I despise your festivals” (5:21). The prophet himself breaks into hymns of praise, and calls the people to seek the LORD, which he defines as “Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the courts” (5:15).

qa.question: What are the visions of Amos?
qa.answer: Five visions in chapters 7–9. In the first two, a swarm of locusts and a consuming fire, Amos prays “How can Jacob survive? He is so small”, and the LORD relents. In the third the Lord stands by a wall with a plumb line, the builder’s test for what is straight, and judgment is fixed. The fourth, a basket of summer fruit, rests on a pun: the Hebrew for summer fruit, qayits, sounds like qets, “end”. In the fifth Amos sees the Lord standing at the altar, commanding the shrine to be struck down.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
